Module functions are perfect when each keyword stands alone. But some keywords
need to **remember** things between calls — a cart that accumulates items, a
client that stays logged in. For that you write a **class**.

Robot Framework imports the class and calls its `@keyword`-decorated methods.
The `@library(scope=...)` decorator controls how long one instance lives:
`scope="TEST"` gives every test a **fresh** instance, so state never leaks
between tests. Reach for state only when keywords genuinely share it — a
stateless module library is simpler when it fits.

```diagram
stack "@library(scope=...) instance lifetime"
GLOBAL -- one instance for the whole run
SUITE -- a fresh instance per suite
TEST -- a fresh instance per test
note "scope=TEST keeps state from leaking between tests"
```

## Task 1 — A cart that accumulates prices

**Goal:** create `libraries/CartMath.py` — a `TEST`-scoped class `CartMath` with
`add_item_price(price)` that stores a price and `cart_total_should_be(expected)`
that checks the running total. (The file name matches the class name — that is
how Robot Framework finds it.)

Here is the same shape over different data — a scoreboard. Adapt it to a cart of
prices.

<!-- example -->
```python
from robot.api.deco import keyword, library


@library(scope="TEST")
class ScoreBoard:
    def __init__(self):
        self.points = []

    @keyword
    def add_points(self, points: int):
        self.points.append(points)

    @keyword
    def score_should_be(self, expected: int):
        actual = sum(self.points)
        if actual != expected:
            raise AssertionError(f"Score {actual}, expected {expected}")
```
<!-- /example -->

**Check:** `libraries/CartMath.py` defines a `CartMath` class whose methods are Robot keywords.

<!-- hint -->
Decorate the class with `@library(scope="TEST")` and give it
`def __init__(self): self.prices = []`.
<!-- /hint -->
<!-- hint -->
Decorate each method with `@keyword`. `add_item_price` appends to `self.prices`;
`cart_total_should_be` compares `sum(self.prices)` to `expected` and raises on a
mismatch.
<!-- /hint -->
<!-- solution -->
```python
from robot.api.deco import keyword, library


@library(scope="TEST")
class CartMath:
    def __init__(self):
        self.prices = []

    @keyword
    def add_item_price(self, price: float):
        self.prices.append(price)

    @keyword
    def cart_total_should_be(self, expected: float):
        actual = sum(self.prices)
        if actual != expected:
            raise AssertionError(f"Cart total {actual}, expected {expected}")
```
<!-- /solution -->

## Task 2 — Import it and run it green

Create `checks/cart.robot`:

```robotframework
*** Settings ***
Library    ../libraries/CartMath.py

*** Test Cases ***
Cart Adds Up
    Add Item Price    19.90
    Add Item Price    12.00
    Cart Total Should Be    31.90
```

Run it:

```bash
uv run robot checks/cart.robot
```

**Check:** the test `Cart Adds Up` passes.
